newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA TRADE FEARS CAP ON NON-BASMATI RICE EXPORTS.
newsitem.headline: INDIA TRADE FEARS CAP ON NON-BASMATI RICE EXPORTS.

text.p: Indian rice exporters said on Thursday they feared a federal government ceiling on exports of non-Basmati rice to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.

"The government is planning to put non-Basmati rice exports under licence for limiting exports," Mulraj Tanna, a leading Bombay rice exporter, told Reuters. "If it happens, it will badly affect India's image as a rice exporter."
Tanna said the government felt domestic rice prices were rising due to a fall in supplies. India currently allows free exports of non-Basmati rice.

"The government is contemplating on a ceiling but I don't think there is a need for a ceiling on non-Basmati exports as supplies were not low," Rashmi Bhimjayani, another leading Bombay foodgrains exporter, told Reuters.
Government officials could not be reached for comment.
Bhimjayani said a surge in export demand for some grades of rice had pushed up prices. "That is why the government is thinking of the ceiling."
Traders said Indian five percent broken non-Basmati rice was quoted at $305-315 fob per tonne, 10 percent at $295-305, 15 percent at $275-285 and 25 percent at $250-260.
"Export demand is very bullish," Bhimjayani said. There were constant shipments of parboiled rice as India was the only country selling the variety.
Traders said export demand was mainly from Nigeria, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. "Export contracts for at least 100,000 tonnes were signed in the last 10 days," Bhimjayani said.
Traders said there was also strong demand for the 100 percent broken variety as Indian prices were much lower than those of Vietnam, the only other supplier.
"The buyers are looking to India as Vietnam prices for 100 percent broken grades were much higher," Bhimjayani said. "This in turn has pushed up Indian prices to some extent."
Traders said Indian 100 percent broken rice was quoted at $185 per tonne compared with Vietnam rice of the same variety quoted at $220.
Industry officials said sowing of the new rice crop was almost over in all the major growing regions and a good crop was expected.
"Sowing is going on very well," Tanna said. "We expect a (winter) crop of about 65 million tonnes."
The country harvests two rice crops, getting the bulk of its output from the winter crop. India harvested about 80 million tonnes in 1996/97 (July-June).

Anil Adlakha, executive director of the All India Rice Exporters Association, said the trade had set an export target of about two million tonnes of non-Basmati rice and about 450,000 tonnes of Basmati rice in 1997/98 (April-March), the same as last year.
